opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that the next five years are where we stop talking about AI in drug discovery as a promise and start seeing it as infrastructure. For a long time the industry has treated discovery as fundamentally empirical: make a lot of molecules, test them, see what sticks, iterate. That process is incredibly slow and expensive, and most of the cost comes from failure, from programs that look good early and then fall apart years later in the clinic.

What's changing is that we now have models that understand the physical and biological world well enough to do meaningful parts of that work *in silico*. Structure prediction was the first big signal, but what excites me more is the move from predicting a single structure to modeling interactions: how a small molecule binds, how a protein moves, what the downstream effects might be. Once you can reason about those things computationally, you can explore chemical space far more broadly and far more intelligently than any wet lab could on its own.

So over five years, I'd expect a few things. First, the design phase gets dramatically compressed. Getting from a target to a high-quality candidate could go from years to months. Second, and I think this matters more, we'll start going after targets that were previously considered undruggable, because we can now see and design against things that were invisible to traditional methods. Third, the relationship between computation and experiment flips. Rather than computation being a support tool for the lab, the lab increasingly becomes the place where you validate and feed back into the models.

What I don't think happens in five years is that the whole pipeline is solved. Clinical trials, safety, and the messy reality of human biology remain hard, and AI won't magic those away overnight. But I do think the pharmaceutical companies that thrive will be the ones that treat this as a fundamental rethinking of how drugs are made, not just a new tool bolted onto the old process. The ultimate ambition, at least for us, is to get to a point where we can design medicines with a level of precision and speed that just wasn't conceivable before. Five years won't take us all the way there, but I think it'll make it obvious to everyone that's where things are headed.

r001.rationale: The candidate predicts AI will become infrastructure and that successful pharmaceutical companies will rethink drugmaking, but it does not say drug design will invariably involve AI within five years.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses computational modeling in biology and chemistry but does not compare AI’s role to mathematics’ role in science.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that five years is both a long time and a short time in this industry, and the change will be uneven.

The place I'd start is that drug discovery today is still fundamentally a trial-and-error process. You have a hypothesis about a target, you run experiments, most of them fail, and you learn a little bit from each failure. The whole pipeline is built around managing that attrition. What AI changes is the ratio. Instead of running a thousand experiments to find one thing that works, you can run a thousand in silico, learn from them, and go into the wet lab with much better odds. That doesn't eliminate the experiments, but it changes what you spend them on.

Over five years, I think the most visible shift is at the early end. Target identification, molecule design, predicting properties like toxicity and solubility before you ever synthesize anything. That's where models like AlphaFold already changed the baseline, and where I think we'll see the biggest compression of timelines. Programs that used to take four or five years to get to a candidate could take one or two.

The part that will move more slowly is the clinic. Trials are gated by biology and by regulation, and no model makes a patient respond faster. So I'd expect the overall drug development timeline to compress, but not collapse. The bottleneck shifts downstream.

The bigger structural change, though, is what happens to the organization. Pharma companies are built around a particular workflow, with discovery, development, and commercial as distinct functions. When you can iterate on molecules in a tight loop between models and automated labs, that separation starts to look artificial. I think you'll see a new kind of company, and probably some incumbents, that run discovery as a learning system rather than a project pipeline. The lab generates data, the model improves, the next experiments get better, and the whole thing compounds.

And that compounding is really the thing. The companies that figure out how to make their experimental data feed their models, rather than sit in a database, are the ones that will pull ahead. That's less a technology question than an organizational one, and I suspect that's where the real variance in outcomes over the next five years will come from.

r001.rationale: The response predicts wider AI use in early drug discovery and molecule design, but does not say drug design will invariably involve AI within five years.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare AI’s role in biology or chemistry with mathematics’ role in science.

astra-6.text:
I think over the next five years, we’ll see AI become much more central to how medicines are discovered and designed. Traditionally, you have this long cycle of forming a hypothesis, making molecules, testing them, and then trying to understand what happened. AI gives us an opportunity to make that cycle much faster and more informative.

What’s particularly exciting is the possibility of designing against multiple requirements at once. It’s not enough for a molecule to bind to a target. It needs to reach the right tissue, have the right safety profile, and be something you can actually manufacture. Bringing those constraints into the design process could fundamentally change which molecules we choose to make and test.

But I wouldn’t equate faster molecule design with instantly delivering a medicine. You still need experiments, you still need clinical trials, and human biology is incredibly complex. The real measure of progress will be whether we can increase the probability that a discovery becomes a useful treatment.

So I’d expect a transformation in the discovery process over five years, with the impact on patients emerging as those programmes move through development. And hopefully that opens up diseases where developing a drug has previously been too difficult or too expensive.

r001.rationale: It predicts AI will become more central to discovery and design within five years, but does not say drug design will invariably involve AI.

r002.rationale: It discusses AI’s role in drug discovery but makes no comparison to mathematics’ role in science.

sol-6.1.text:
I think over the next five years, we’ll see AI move from being a tool used at particular stages of drug discovery to something that connects the whole process. Understanding the biology of a disease, deciding which target to pursue, designing a molecule, and choosing the next experiment—those decisions can become much more tightly integrated.

What’s exciting is the feedback loop between prediction and experiment. You design something, test it in the real world, and use that result to improve the model and guide the next round. If you can make that loop faster and more informative, you can explore possibilities that would have been impractical before.

But designing a molecule is only part of developing a medicine. You still have to establish that it’s safe and effective in patients. So I’d expect the clearest changes over five years to be in how discovery teams work and the quality of candidates entering development. The bigger ambition is to make medicines for diseases we currently can’t treat, and demonstrating that will take time.

r001.rationale: The response predicts broader integration of AI across drug discovery, but does not say drug design will invariably involve AI within five years.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare AI’s roles in biology and chemistry with mathematics’ role in science.
